Getting the spent nuclear fuel off our coastline has been a top priority of mine for as long as I've served in Congress, and it will stay that way for as long as it takes. There is no question that this fuel needs to move as quickly and safely as possible.

When I got to Congress in 2019, there was no plan to move it. 

The federal government was supposed to start taking this waste in 1998 and never did. 

Yucca Mountain, the only site Congress ever picked, was shut down in 2009, and nothing replaced it. Months before I took office, a canister nearly fell 18 feet during loading. In sum, I inherited a bad situation.

One of my first steps was bringing experts and community leaders together on a SONGS Task Force. They presented findings and recommendations that have guided my work ever since.

I brought Democrats and Republicans together in the Spent Nuclear Fuel Solutions Caucus to restart a stalled national conversation. I’ve met regularly with Department of Energy staff, including earlier this week, to discuss the new path forward.

Through the House Appropriations process, I've helped secure over $250 million for this work. 

That includes Atlas, a new railcar built to carry spent fuel safely across the country by rail. The funding we secured supported the last administration's work to find willing host communities through a collaborative siting program. It also is assisting the new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, a continuation of this work, with six states already signing up.

I’ve also introduced several pieces of bipartisan legislation that provide a strong roadmap for the future, including language to prioritize the movement of spent fuel from sites like ours, and to create a new sole purpose entity for the management of spent fuel nationwide.

There is much work ahead, but I’m greatly encouraged by our progress. 

I'll be sharing a more comprehensive update in coming weeks.

One of the most powerful experiences I’ve had in 21 months as your Member of Congress was visiting the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency at Pearl Harbor and seeing firsthand the commitment our nation has made to identify, bring home, and reunite missing servicemembers with their families. On National POW/MIA Recognition Day, we honor the brave men and women who were held captive or who are still missing in their service to our country – including many of whom were never given a proper chance to be laid to rest. 

To this day, over 900 Marylanders who served in World War I, World War II, Korea, and Vietnam have been declared missing in action. Today and everyday, we remember the lives lost and stand with the families who never received closure for their loved ones who made the ultimate sacrifice for our freedoms. It’s why I’m committed to fighting to restore vital funding of the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency to continue its most sacred mission. If my office can be of assistance, please reach out to (410) 832-8890.
